mma_rules_scoring.summary: MMA is a round-based combat sport where current Unified Rules scoring prioritizes damaging/effective legal striking and effective grappling results over activity volume or static control.
core_rules: Professional Unified Rules rounds are five minutes with one minute rest; bouts may be scheduled from one to five rounds and cannot exceed five rounds or 25 minutes.
The referee is the sole in-bout authority to stop a contest; doctor, corner, and referee stoppages affect official result pathways.
Three judges use the 10-point must system unless a promotion or amateur rule set specifies otherwise.
Effective striking is judged by the damage/effect of legal strikes; effective grappling is judged by impactful results from takedowns, submission attempts, reversals, and advantageous positions.
Effective aggressiveness and fighting-area control are tie-breakers only when effective striking/grappling does not separate the round.
10-9 indicates a close round win; 10-8 requires a large margin involving damage with dominance and/or duration; 10-7 indicates complete domination where stoppage is warranted.
Static control is not enough: dominant grappling must lead toward damage, submissions, positional advancement, or sustained effective offense.
Current Unified Rules prohibit knees or kicks to the head of a grounded opponent; grounded means any body part other than hands or feet touches the canvas.

Key fouls include headbutts, eye gouging, biting/spitting, hair pulling, fish hooking, spikes onto head/neck, strikes to spine/back of head, throat attacks, outstretched fingers toward eyes, groin attacks, stomping grounded opponents, fence/glove/shorts grabbing for control, small joint manipulation, attacks after bell or on break, and corner interference.
Rules can vary by jurisdiction, amateur federation, and promotion; backend output must confirm rule set before allowing borderline techniques.
backend_implications: Tag scoring lessons by damage, dominance, duration, effective_grappling, aggressiveness, and area_control.
Do not equate volume statistics with round-winning impact.
Generate rules-aware constraints for grounded opponent, fence work, submissions, and amateur-pro distinctions.
Surface local-rule verification whenever user mentions competition, sparring under event rules, or promotion-specific preparation.

fight_phases.summary: MMA phases shift between open-space striking, clinch/fence, takedown transition, ground control, submission threat, ground striking, scramble, referee reset, and corner rest.
phase_principles: Each phase has different scoring value, risk, energy cost, and safety constraints.
Transitions decide many exchanges: striking entries must include takedown awareness, and grappling exits must include strike-defense awareness.
Fence phase is a distinct tactical environment: head position, underhooks, wrist control, stance, and hip position determine offense and escape.
Ground phase must separate control from offense; app scoring education should reward damage, submissions, advancement, and meaningful positional improvement.
backend_implications: Session design should alternate phase isolation, transition drills, and integrated rounds.
Use round timers and phase-specific constraints instead of generic conditioning alone.
Store user weaknesses by phase so plans can target the highest-leverage missing link.

range_management.summary: MMA range is not only long, mid, and close; it also includes takedown threat, fence geometry, grounded states, and rule-set legality.
backend_implications: Range drills need both offensive goal and defensive exit.
Do not prescribe kicking-heavy entries without takedown defense context.
Grounded-opponent legality must be attached to range and ruleset.

tactical_iq.summary: MMA tactical IQ is the ability to select risk-adjusted actions by score state, rule set, opponent pattern, phase, fatigue, and available exits.
tactical_rules: If ahead, prioritize clean damaging actions, positional safety, exits, and avoiding unnecessary scrambles.
If behind, increase initiative with layered entries and finish threats rather than reckless volume.
Do not enter on a straight line without a planned exit, angle, frame, clinch, or level-change follow-up.
Use feints to collect reactions before committing to high-cost kicks, shots, or extended combinations.
Against wrestlers, strike with stance recovery, underhook awareness, and fence escape routes.
Against strikers, change level, force clinch decisions, and create grappling threats without shooting from too far away.
Against submission threats, prioritize posture, elbow-knee connection, hand-fighting, and safe disengagement before ground-and-pound volume.
Corner feedback should be translated into one primary adjustment and one emergency cue, not a long list.
backend_implications: Assess tactical IQ with scenario prompts, constrained sparring, and video-review tags.
Store tactical patterns as if_then rules by phase and opponent archetype.
Generate round scenarios that include score state and fatigue rather than neutral drills only.

competition_week.summary: Competition week is for rule confirmation, recovery, timing, weight-class compliance, medical readiness, and tactical simplicity, not major skill acquisition.
fight_week_priorities: Confirm rule set, jurisdiction, equipment, weigh-in time, hydration rules if applicable, round count, and amateur/pro restrictions.
Reduce hard contact and high-fatigue grappling while preserving speed, timing, mobility, and confidence.
Avoid new techniques, new sparring partners, new supplements, and untested weight-management tactics.
Use short technical rounds, pad timing, wrestling-wall entries at low impact, mobility, and recovery monitoring.
Track sleep, stress, soreness, head symptoms, hand/wrist pain, skin issues, and weight-management strain.
Make weight and hydration through qualified coach/medical/nutrition support; app must not prescribe aggressive dehydration or sauna protocols.
Post weigh-in, prioritize supervised rehydration/refueling, low-stress movement, rules meeting, hand wrap logistics, and mental rehearsal.
After the bout, medical checks and symptoms override planned return to training.
backend_implications: Fight-week plans should taper contact before tapering all movement.
Competition-week sessions need explicit contact_intensity, round_count, and stop_conditions.
Any user input suggesting severe dehydration, fainting, confusion, concussion symptoms, or inability to make weight should trigger safety messaging and professional referral.

technical_principles.principle: Scoring favors damaging/effective legal actions and impactful grappling results, not raw strike count or passive control.
coaching_cues: make the action change the opponent

technical_principles.principle: Dominant positions matter most when they create damage, submissions, positional advancement, or sustained defensive reactions.
Every entry should include an exit, angle, frame, clinch tie, or level-change follow-up.
MMA striking must account for takedown threat; stance, kick choice, combination length, and fence location all change under wrestling pressure.
Fence work is its own phase with unique scoring, fatigue, and escape demands.
coaching_cues: do not reach behind for fence

technical_principles.principle: In scrambles, the first stable control point often matters more than a flashy attack.
Technique legality changes by professional Unified Rules, amateur rules, promotion, and jurisdiction.
Sparring, head contact, hard grappling, and damage exposure must be tracked separately from total training volume.
Fight week should preserve timing and decision confidence while reducing fatigue, hard contact, and novelty.
Head symptoms, visual disturbance, confusion, fainting, severe pain, uncontrolled bleeding, or unsafe dehydration override any generated session.

primary_goals: Understand basic rules, legal targets, tap etiquette, and stop commands.
Build stance, guard, footwork, breakfalls, safe partner habits, and no-contact or touch-contact striking mechanics.
Learn positional safety: frames, shrimping, technical stand-up, posture in guard, basic underhooks, and fence awareness.
beginner.contact_guidance: No hard sparring by default. Use shadow, bag, pads, drilling, positional games, touch sparring, and coach-supervised grappling with clear tap and stop rules.
avoid: Heel hooks, neck cranks, uncontrolled slams, hard head contact, unsupervised sparring, ego-based rolling, and competition weight cuts.
Learning advanced offense before defensive responsibility and escape routes.
progress_markers: Can follow referee-style commands and stop immediately.
Can keep stance after basic strikes and recover guard after contact.
Can tap early and respect partner taps.
Can explain illegal actions for grounded opponents and common fouls.

primary_goals: Integrate striking entries with takedown defense and clinch transitions.
Use constrained sparring to solve range, fence, top/bottom, and scramble problems.
Understand current scoring criteria and train damage-aware, position-to-offense decision making.
intermediate.contact_guidance: Technical and controlled sparring may be used with coach oversight, matched partners, protective equipment, round limits, and symptom gates.
avoid: Kicking without stance recovery against wrestlers.
Playing passive top control that would not score under current criteria.
Preparing for competition without confirming rule set and amateur restrictions.
progress_markers: Can enter and exit combinations under takedown threat.
Can defend fence takedowns and return to center.
Can win or recover from common scrambles without exposing neck or back.
Can adapt one tactical cue between rounds.

primary_goals: Build opponent-specific game plans by stance, range preference, takedown chain, submission threats, and score-state behavior.
Periodize contact, hard grappling, S&C, conditioning, recovery, and technical sharpness around camp phase.
Use high-fidelity round scenarios: ahead, behind, hurt, tired, late-round fence, defending submission, and needing a finish.
advanced.contact_guidance: Open sparring and fight-simulation rounds require planned exposure, medical readiness, trusted partners, rule-set constraints, and adequate recovery spacing.
avoid: Adding new high-risk tactics in fight week.
Using damage-heavy rounds to test toughness.
Ignoring weight-management stress or concussion symptoms.
Assuming UFC/Unified, IMMAF, and ONE rules are interchangeable.
progress_markers: Can adjust tactics by scoring state and opponent archetype.
Can use feints to draw predictable reactions across phases.
Can convert fence control into damage, takedown, or safe disengagement.
Can taper while maintaining timing and confidence.

drills_or_practice_design.name: Scoring Lens Round Review
drills_or_practice_design.design: Watch or simulate a short round and tag damage/effect, effective grappling, aggressiveness, and area control in that order.
constraints: No winner chosen by volume alone
Passive control must be marked separately from effective offense
drills_or_practice_design.progression: Move from coach-led examples to athlete self-scoring and corner adjustment selection.

drills_or_practice_design.name: Entry-Exit Touch Rounds
drills_or_practice_design.design: One athlete enters with a two-strike combination; every entry must finish with an angle, frame, clinch tie, or level-change feint.
constraints: Reset if athlete exits straight back with hands down
drills_or_practice_design.progression: Add takedown threat, fence boundary, and score-state targets.

drills_or_practice_design.name: Kick-Stance-Sprawl Recovery
drills_or_practice_design.design: Athlete throws controlled kicks, immediately recovers stance, then reacts to partner shot cue with sprawl, underhook, or angle-off.
constraints: Athlete must regain stance before reset
drills_or_practice_design.progression: Add feints, cage line, and counter-strike after defense.

drills_or_practice_design.name: Fence Underhook Escape Series
drills_or_practice_design.design: Start with back near fence; athlete wins inside position, turns hips, pummels underhook, and exits to center or reverses.
constraints: Head position and balance prioritized over strength
drills_or_practice_design.progression: Add mat return defense, knees to body where legal, and 30-second score-state scenarios.

drills_or_practice_design.name: Top Control Must Create Offense
drills_or_practice_design.design: Top athlete starts in half guard or side control and scores only for posture, safe strikes, pass attempts, submission threats, or improved position.
constraints: No head contact for novice groups
Bottom athlete wins by guard recovery, stand-up, sweep, or safe tie-up
drills_or_practice_design.progression: Add timed scoring, referee stand-up warning, and judging criteria review.

drills_or_practice_design.name: Scramble To First Stable Control
drills_or_practice_design.design: Start from turtle, front headlock, single-leg shelf, or failed shot; goal is first stable control without exposing neck or back.
constraints: Reset on uncontrolled roll or slam risk
drills_or_practice_design.progression: Add cage wall, strike posture cues, and late-round fatigue.

drills_or_practice_design.name: Score-State Constraint Rounds
drills_or_practice_design.design: Run short rounds where athlete is told they are ahead, even, behind, hurt, or needing a finish.
constraints: One tactical objective only per round
drills_or_practice_design.progression: Add corner feedback and require athlete to verbalize adjustment before next round.

drills_or_practice_design.name: Fight-Week Technical Sharpener
drills_or_practice_design.design: Short low-contact session using warm-up, mobility, pad timing, low-amplitude wrestling entries, one game-plan sequence, and cooldown.
constraints: Stop for head symptoms, unusual fatigue, hand pain, or weight-cut distress
drills_or_practice_design.progression: Reduce volume and keep speed/timing as competition day approaches.

common_errors.error: Assuming more strikes or longer top time automatically wins the round.
common_errors.why_it_matters: Current scoring values damage/effect and effective grappling results before volume or area control.
common_errors.correction: Teach athletes to identify which actions changed the opponent, created submission risk, or forced sustained defense.

common_errors.error: Holding a superior position without advancing, damaging, or threatening a finish.
common_errors.why_it_matters: Officials can stand fighters up, and passive control is weak under scoring criteria.
common_errors.correction: Require position-to-offense goals in ground drills.

common_errors.error: Throwing long combinations or naked kicks without stance recovery or underhook awareness.
common_errors.why_it_matters: MMA striking exchanges can become wrestling exchanges instantly.
common_errors.correction: Attach sprawl, frame, angle, or clinch follow-up to striking drills.

common_errors.error: Exiting exchanges straight backward, especially near the fence.
common_errors.why_it_matters: This concedes cage position and can turn striking defense into takedown defense under pressure.
common_errors.correction: Train angle exits, pivots, frames, and center recovery.

common_errors.error: Treating sparring and rolling as toughness tests rather than technical learning.
common_errors.why_it_matters: Late taps and uncontrolled escalation increase joint, neck, and concussion risk.
common_errors.correction: Use early tap culture, matched partners, clear constraints, and coach stop authority.

common_errors.error: Training as if all MMA promotions and amateur competitions use identical legality and scoring.
common_errors.why_it_matters: Unified Rules, IMMAF amateur rules, ONE rules, and local commissions can differ.
common_errors.correction: Confirm rule set before fight camp and tag plans by event_ruleset.

common_errors.error: Using hard sparring or high-fatigue grappling close to competition to feel ready.
common_errors.why_it_matters: Fight week should reduce accumulated fatigue and contact exposure while preserving timing.
common_errors.correction: Use short technical sharpener rounds and recovery monitoring.

common_errors.error: Trying untested dehydration, sauna, supplement, or diet methods during competition week.
common_errors.why_it_matters: Rapid weight loss can impair performance and create medical risk.
common_errors.correction: Use qualified professional support and do not generate aggressive weight-cut prescriptions.

safety_constraints.constraint: Headache, dizziness, confusion, visual symptoms, loss of consciousness, unusual fatigue, nausea, or behavior change stops contact and requires medical evaluation before return.
Hard sparring is never a default beginner or general-conditioning prescription and requires coach supervision, matched partners, rules, protective equipment, and recovery spacing.
Do not prescribe dehydration, sauna, diuretics, extreme fluid restriction, or last-minute rapid weight-loss protocols.

Remove or constrain techniques illegal under the user's rule set, especially grounded-opponent head attacks, spikes, small-joint manipulation, neck cranks, heel hooks, elbows in amateur rules, and fence grabbing.
All submission, grappling, and partner-contact drills require immediate release on tap, verbal tap, scream, referee/coach stop, or safety cue.
Large skill, size, strength, or intensity mismatches increase injury risk in sparring and wrestling rounds.
Wall work, mat returns, throws, and slams require controlled landings, breakfall skill, and no spike mechanics.
Open wounds, suspicious skin infections, uncontrolled bleeding, or poor hygiene should stop partner contact until medically cleared.
Competition-week programming should reduce hard contact, maximal grappling fatigue, and novelty while maintaining timing and confidence.

sport_training_rules.rule: Prioritize damage/effect from legal striking and impactful grappling results before activity volume, aggressiveness, or area control.
Do not score or reinforce static control unless it advances position, creates damage, threatens submission, or forces sustained defensive reactions.
Use five-minute rounds, one-minute rests, and a maximum of five rounds or 25 fight minutes in a 24-hour period unless local rules specify otherwise.
Ask or infer event ruleset before permitting techniques that vary across Unified Rules, amateur rules, ONE, and local commissions.
Under current Unified Rules, block knees or kicks to the head when the opponent is grounded; grounded means any body part other than hands or feet is on the canvas.
Every entry must finish with a defensive responsibility: angle, guard return, frame, clinch tie, level change, sprawl readiness, or reset.
When takedown threat is present, kicking drills must include stance recovery, sprawl/underhook cue, and fence-location awareness.
Treat fence work as its own phase with underhook, head position, hip position, wrist control, legal pressure, and escape objectives.
In scrambles, prioritize neck safety, inside position, hip control, and first stable control before risky submissions or strikes.
Translate corner feedback into one primary tactical adjustment and one emergency cue.

planning_rules.rule: Track sparring rounds, contact intensity, head contact, hard grappling, partner mismatch, and post-session symptoms separately from total workload.
Default to no-contact, touch-contact, pads, bag, positional games, and coach-supervised low-intensity grappling.
Reduce hard sparring, high-fatigue grappling, and novelty; preserve timing, speed, mobility, and simple tactical rehearsal.
Collect event ruleset, amateur/pro status, round count, weigh-in protocol, equipment, and local commission constraints before generating competition-specific sessions.
Do not generate aggressive dehydration or rapid weight-loss instructions; provide safety constraints and recommend qualified medical/sports nutrition support.
Cancel contact and refer for medical review when concussion-like symptoms, fainting, uncontrolled bleeding, severe pain, or unsafe dehydration signs appear.
Return through symptom check, restoration, low-contact skill, conditioning, strength, then contact only after readiness and clearance.
Include open-space striking, clinch/fence, takedown transition, ground top/bottom, scramble, and recovery instead of overloading one phase.

teaching_progressions.success_criteria: Athlete can train safely with partner, stop instantly, tap early, and explain common illegal actions.
Athlete can enter and exit without crossing feet, dropping hands, or conceding easy takedown.
Athlete defends initial shot and returns to center or creates safe offense.
Athlete can reduce damage risk from bottom and create a path back to neutral or offense.
Athlete can convert fence position into a scoring action or escape without fouling.
Athlete chooses risk-adjusted actions based on time, score, damage, phase, and opponent threat.
Athlete arrives sharp, rule-aware, medically ready, and not overloaded by new tactics or contact.

skill_assessments.method: Ask athlete to identify legal targets, grounded-opponent restrictions, common fouls, scoring hierarchy, and 10-8 criteria.
skill_assessments.pass_signal: Correctly explains damage/effective grappling priority and at least five major fouls for their rule set.

skill_assessments.method: Observe five controlled entries from each side with required exit, guard return, stance recovery, and takedown awareness.
skill_assessments.pass_signal: At least four of five entries finish balanced with defensive responsibility and no straight-back drift into fence.

skill_assessments.method: Start with back near fence for 30 seconds; athlete must win inside position, avoid fence grab, and exit or reverse.
skill_assessments.pass_signal: Maintains posture, wins underhook or frame, protects hips, and returns to center safely.

skill_assessments.method: Start bottom half guard or closed guard with top applying controlled pressure; bottom must protect head and recover guard, stand, sweep, or tie up.
skill_assessments.pass_signal: Limits clean contact lanes and creates a credible escape or reversal pathway.

skill_assessments.method: Top athlete has 60 seconds to create pass, posture, safe strikes, submission threat, or improved position from half guard.
skill_assessments.pass_signal: Creates effective offense without relying on static pinning.

skill_assessments.method: Start from failed shot, front headlock, turtle, or single-leg shelf; assess neck safety, hip control, and first stable control.
skill_assessments.pass_signal: Protects neck and back while securing stable position or safe disengagement.

skill_assessments.method: Run three short scenario rounds: ahead, behind, and late-round even; athlete states plan before and adjustment after.
skill_assessments.pass_signal: Plan matches score state and avoids unnecessary risk when ahead or panic volume when behind.

skill_assessments.method: Check sleep, soreness, head symptoms, hand/wrist pain, neck pain, weight-management strain, partner match, and recent contact load.
skill_assessments.pass_signal: No red flags, clear contact objective, appropriate partner, and coach-defined stop conditions.
